# Bāhitika Sutta (MN 88 (PTS MN ii 112))

**ID:** MN 88 (PTS MN ii 112)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Bāhitika Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Foreign Cloth
**PTS:** MN ii 112
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn88
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bāhitika Sutta* (MN 88; PTS MN ii 112) is the eighty-eighth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, known in English translation as "The Foreign Cloth" [SuttaCentral] or "The Cloak Discourse" [Edelglass and Garfield 2009]. Set on the road near Sāvatthī, the narrative depicts King Pasenadi of Kosala sending a messenger to inquire if Venerable Ānanda is available, after which the king formally approaches on an elephant, dismounts, and proceeds on foot to question him on ethics [Galasek 2016]. Pasenadi asks what bodily, verbal, and mental conduct is censured or praised by the Buddha and wise recluses and brahmins [SuttaCentral; Goodman 2009]. Ānanda defines unwholesome and blameworthy behavior as actions that bring harm, ripen in pain, cause affliction to oneself or others, and increase unwholesome qualities while diminishing wholesome ones, whereas blameless, skillful actions produce the reverse [Edelglass and Garfield 2009; Goodman 2009]. Highly pleased, Pasenadi presents Ānanda with a foreign cloth or cloak (*bāhitikā*) that he had previously received from King Ajātasattu of Magadha [SuttaCentral; Radich 2011].

In Theravāda scholasticism, the sutta is famous for establishing the canonical definition of *kusala* as "faultless" or "blameless" (*anavajja*); Buddhaghosa and subsequent Abhidhamma commentators refer to this specific semantic definition as the "Bāhitika-sutta method of exposition" (*bāhitikasuttanta-naya*), distinguishing it from the sense of health (associated with the Jātakas) and mental skill (associated with the Abhidhamma) [Cousins 1996; Edelglass and Garfield 2009]. Modern ethicists have examined the sutta's chain of definitions as evidence for a consequentialist or two-part objective list theory of well-being in early Buddhist ethics [Goodman 2009]. Commentarial tradition in the *Papañcasūdanī* connects the occasion of Pasenadi's questioning with the slander incident surrounding the ascetic Sundarī [Galasek 2016].

SuttaCentral notes a direct Chinese parallel in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 214), which has been translated and analyzed in comparative studies by Bhikkhu Anālayo [SuttaCentral; Bingenheimer et al. 2013]. Machine text alignment by DharmaNexus corroborates this correspondence in the *Madhyama-āgama* (ZH_T01_0026) alongside partial alignments with texts such as the *Ajitasenavyākaraṇa* and *Mahākarmavibhaṅga* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus detects 1,652 matching segments across 111 texts, demonstrating substantial reuse of doctrinal phrasing with the *Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 61, sharing over 11,000 characters, notably §14.10–14.11), the *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47), and *Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta* (MN 114) [DharmaNexus].
